A plinth is a flat, solid block — usually square or rectangular — that sits at the very bottom of something, supporting it from below. Its purpose is to elevate and support: it lifts an object off the ground, gives it a stable base, and makes it look more prominent, formal, or important.

Think of a thick, flat brick. Now imagine placing a statue on top of it. That block the statue stands on is essentially a plinth. It's always the lowest element — the "ground floor" of a structure or object.

Under statues and sculptures — this is the most common use today. When you see a statue in a public square or park, the stone block the statue stands on is the plinth. It raises the figure above eye level so it can be seen from a distance and carries a sense of dignity and grandeur. Similarly, in art galleries and museums, the plain white cube or block that a sculpture sits on is called a plinth. The plinth keeps the artwork at a viewable height and separates it visually from the floor.

In classical architecture, under columns — in grand old buildings with tall columns (like ancient Greek temples, courthouses, or banks), the very base of each column rests on a plinth. It's the flat slab at the absolute bottom, beneath everything else in the column. The whole column rises up from it.

At the base of a building's walls — in construction, the lowest part of an exterior wall — the section just above the ground that sometimes projects slightly outward — is also called a plinth or a plinth course. It helps protect the wall from water splashing off the ground and gives the building a visually heavier, grounded look at its base.

Under furniture — kitchen cabinets, wardrobes, and other large fitted furniture often sit on a plinth, which is a low base panel running along the bottom. It conceals the gap between the furniture and the floor and gives the unit a clean, finished appearance.

On a record player (turntable) — the flat board or chassis that forms the body of a turntable — the part the motor, spindle, and spinning plate are mounted onto — is called the plinth. It's the base that houses and holds everything together.

A plinth is almost always simple in form. It's flat on top (so whatever sits on it is stable), wider than it is tall, and tends to be plain and undecorated — because its job is to support and display, not to compete visually with whatever is above it. It can be made of stone, marble, concrete, wood, metal, or other solid materials depending on the context.
Plinth vs. pedestal — an important distinction

These two words are sometimes confused and occasionally used interchangeably in everyday speech, so it's worth understanding the difference.

A pedestal is a tall support — almost like a short column or pillar — that elevates a statue or object. It can be quite high.

A plinth is the flat, lowest-most slab at the base of something. In fact, a pedestal itself often rests on a plinth. So a plinth can be part of a pedestal (its very bottom), or it can exist independently as a simple flat base with nothing more to it.

The practical difference: a pedestal is a tall, prominent display stand; a plinth is specifically the flat, foundational block at the bottom. In everyday casual use, though, people often call a statue's base a "plinth" whether it's purely flat or has some height to it.

Occasionally you'll encounter "plinth" used metaphorically in formal or literary writing to mean the foundation on which something abstract rests. For example: "Justice is the plinth on which all other rights stand." This is not a common use, but it follows naturally from the word's core meaning — a solid base that holds something up.
A plinth is the stable, flat block at the very bottom of something — it supports what's above it, elevates it off the ground, and gives it a solid, grounded foundation.
